newsitem.title: UK: At least 45 van Goghs may be fakes - art paper.
newsitem.headline: At least 45 van Goghs may be fakes - art paper.

text.p: At least 45 paintings and drawings by Vincent van Gogh may be fakes, a leading London-based art review said on Friday.

One of the alleged fakes is "Sunflowers", sold to Yasuda Fire & Marine Insurance Co Ltd in 1987 for 24.75 million pounds ($41.46 million), earning the company a rebuke from Japan's finance ministry for "an excessive demonstration of wealth".

The Art Newspaper also questioned the authenticity of other famous works by the Dutch post-impressionist, including "L'Arlesienne" in New York's Metropolitan Museum and "Dr Gachet" in the Musee D'Orsay in Paris.
Its report, greeted sceptically by at least one expert, said the number of fakes could be as high as 100.
The review bases its allegations on work by Jan Hulsker, a leading van Gogh specialist who issued a new edition of his catalogue of the master's entire works late last year.

Hulsker, interviewed by the review about a rise in the number of works whose origin he questions in the new catalogue, is quoted as questioning 45 and saying he has "very strong doubts about the authenticity of many more works".
Part of the problem, the review said, is that van Gogh failed to sell his works before his suicide in 1890, so there are no contemporary sale records to help authenticate his works.
But as prices for his work soared from the 1920s onwards, fakers were tempted into making a quick killing.

Their task was helped by the fact van Gogh often gave works away or abandoned them. Frequently fakes were based on the artist's descriptions of his work in letters or on preparatory sketches, The Art Newspaper's Martin Bailey reported.
Not everyone has been convinced by the new allegations.

David Lee, editor of the London-based Art Review Magazine, told the BBC: "Stories of van Gogh fakes have been coming out for years and years. There were a huge number of fakes in the 1920s and 30s of paintings by van Gogh because at that time it became profitable to actually fake his work.
"The fascinating thing about this new story is that it's alleged that Dr Gachet, a homeopath looking after van Gogh in the last days of his life, has introduced a few fakes himself.
"I find that very hard to believe because at the time...it wasn't in his interest to fake paintings by van Gogh because they weren't actually worth anything."
A spokesman for the Musee D'Orsay said the museum was aware of reports that the portrait of Dr Gachet may be a fake but still believed it to be a genuine van Gogh.
Van Gogh museum curator Schaar van Heughten told the Dutch ANP news agency: "(The article) represents the sum of opinions of various researchers including Martin Bailey.

"His recent research keeps surfacing in various magazines. We have known for some time that fakes and mistaken attributions exist." But he said works were not immediately put under the microscope if someone disputed their authenticity.
